verdicts.fix: Two votes with at least 13 days in between; legislation not passed by the end of the period dies and must be reintroduced.

Chamber of Commerce v. Seattle, No. 17-35640 (9th Cir. May 11, 2018): state-action immunity did not shield the ordinance from the Sherman Act claim (dismissal reversed and remanded); dismissal of NLRA preemption claims (Machinists and Garmon) affirmed. Primary document; FACT fits.

Texas House bill analysis, SB 2205 (85R, 2017): 'prohibits a political subdivision or a state agency from imposing a franchise or other regulation related to the operation of an automated motor vehicle or automated driving system.' Effective Sept. 1, 2017. Source is a committee bill analysis, not the enacted text.

Rests on one case (Texas preemption of local regulation of AV operation) stated as a general rule. The page itself says a federal rule would 'narrow what any city can require of the cars themselves', not end the local fight; D.C. would still decide permits, fees, caps and labor terms.
verdicts.fix: Where a higher level moves first, it can take the question away from cities, as Texas did in 2017.

May draft: half of per-mile revenue at 15 cents to driver training (Sidley), i.e. 7.5 cents a mile. Nov. 10 draft: 25% of 7.5 cents for three years (Hill Rag), i.e. 1.875 cents a mile. Training money per mile fell by three quarters, not half; the page's own calculator reports about 81% less over four years. Sunset after three years and October 2027 earliest are supported (Hill Rag).
verdicts.fix: The driver training share was cut from half to a quarter of a per-mile charge that was itself halved, so training money per mile fell by three quarters, and it ends after three years, while the cars would not reach the street until late 2027 at the earliest.

Concessions table, Riders row, May column (untagged): 'Not described in coverage we found.' Sidley, a source the page lists for the May draft, describes rider terms: a plan addressing 'disparate availability or wait times' across wards; 'proof of liability coverage'; crash notice to DDOT within 'eight hours after the crash'; a ban on requiring customers to agree to 'mandatory arbitration of liability disputes'. Reason: $5 million insurance. As printed, the table credits the Nov. 10 draft with protections that were already in the May draft, and crash reporting actually loosened from 8 to 12 hours.

flags: Scope: the ledger's 74 items (c001 to c074) were checked, plus 44 tagged claims held in the page's <script> (vote planner rows s-P01 to s-P16, lever-board entries s-L01 to s-L28) and one untagged table cell (t01). The extractor garbles the concessions table (c011 to c021 carry HTML fragments and neighboring cells); each was judged against the cell its tag follows on the rendered page.

Source access: NBC4, WJLA, Hill Rag, The Washington Sun, City Cast, the council schedule PDF, CRS R47927, Akerman, Sidley, Reason, Punchbowl (paywalled past the first lines), IIHS, autoevolution, Legis1, Justia, the Texas bill analysis and Masley were all read through a page-reading tool that paraphrases. Short exact phrases were confirmed one by one; long passages were not seen verbatim. Direct downloads were blocked by the network proxy. The council's bill page (LIMS B26-0684) could not be retrieved (robots disallowed).
Undisclosed outlet conflict (c033, s-P15): Hill Rag says DDOT has 60 days to open driverless testing applications; WUSA9 (Nov. 10, via Yahoo) says 90 days. WUSA9 is not on the page's source list.
Undisclosed outlet conflict, minor: Waymo's city count is 'at least 14' (Hill Rag, per Waymo) vs 'commercial service in 15 cities' (City Cast). 'At least 14' covers both; no fix required.

Undisclosed outlet conflict, minor: City Cast describes the 20-cent per-mile fee as 'kept', which also conflicts with the May draft's 15 cents (Sidley, Reason). The table note mentions City Cast only for the revision. Consider 'City Cast DC reported a 20-cent fee in both drafts'.
Committee vote timing: WJLA and NBC4 say a vote is expected this week; Hill Rag says 'a date has not been set'. The hero's 'Committee vote expected' is fair, but the conflict is not stated.

Process omission (not a tagged claim): Hill Rag says that after committee the bill 'still has to get through the Committee of the Whole, then two Council votes.' The 2026 schedule shows a Committee of the Whole meeting on Nov. 24. The planner and section 01 go straight from committee vote to the Dec. 1 first vote, so 'Week of Nov. 16: on track' may be too generous. c007's hedge partly covers this; the step should be named.

Tag consistency: c010 says the 'what a delay does' lines are Infera's reading, but three of the seven carry REPORTED chips (Allen, The no votes, Unions). For Allen and The no votes the chip covers a reported fact in the same cell and is defensible; for Unions it is the wrong tag (s-L19). Consider putting the reported fact in 'On the record' and keeping the delay line INFERENCE.

c046 context: Masley's 'about 40 traffic deaths a year' is correctly attributed, but WUSA9 quotes Allen that D.C. recorded 25 traffic deaths in 2025 and 36 so far in 2026. A reader may take 40 as current; consider adding the recent figures.

c053: 'a cap written around the one ready company' can read as a claim about drafting intent. No source shows intent, and Waymo objects to the limits (Hill Rag). Consider 'a cap that, in practice, only one company can fill'.

Planner verdict line for 'Not this year' ('Exactly what the mayor-elect and two committee members have asked for') goes a little past the record: they asked to take it up next year (City Cast, Sun), not for the bill to lapse and be reintroduced.
c058: the source prints Allen's question as 'for what?'; the page capitalizes it 'For What?'.

Editorial Standard: a real other side is present (section 07 gives both cases with named sources). The Anthropic conflict note is present and accurate: Waymo is an Alphabet company, and Google invested in Anthropic and competes with it (Bloomberg Law, Apr. 24, 2026).

Disclosure wording (Editorial Standard): the conflict note says the editor 'works in broadcast news' and, separately, that NBC4 'is an NBC station.' If the editor's broadcast work is for NBC or an NBC-related company, say so directly in one sentence rather than leaving readers to connect the two.
No source text addressed to an AI or a reviewer was found in any page read.

Today's checks (Nov. 11, 2026): SELF DRIVE Act still shows no action after the Feb. 10 subcommittee vote; no CARS funder disclosure found; no report of an added December meeting; committee vote not yet reported. All WATCH items remain open.
